en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Requiring Confession (Pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍa)
2. The Second Training Rule on Confession (Pāṭidesanīya) At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, monks were eating after having been invited to the homes of families.
The group-of-six bhikkhunīs stood giving directions to the group-of-six bhikkhus, saying:
"Give soup here; give rice there.
The group-of-six bhikkhus ate as much as they desired.
Other monks did not eat according to their pleasure.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before]... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the group-of-six monks not stop the nuns when they are giving directions?"... [as before]...
“Is it true, monks, that you did not stop the nuns while they were giving directions?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them … [as before] …
"How indeed, you foolish men, could you not stop the bhikkhunīs while they are giving directions?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:"
“Now, when monks are eating after being invited to families, if that bhikkhunī stands there in a manner of offering service,
saying, ‘Give soup here, give rice there,’ those monks should dismiss that bhikkhunī,
saying, ‘Step aside for now, sister, while the monks are eating. If not even a single monk should feel inclined to do so...”
To dissuade that nun, saying, “Sister, please step aside until the monks have finished eating,” those monks must confess:
“Friends, we have committed a blameworthy, unsuitable offense entailing confession; we confess it.
Now, as for the monks who, having been invited to families, are eating...
"Family" refers to four families: the khattiya family, the brāhmaṇa family, the vessa family, and the sudda family.
"Eating when invited" means that they eat having been invited with any one of the five kinds of cooked food.
A bhikkhunī is one who has received full ordination in both Saṅghas.
"Attending upon" means...

"According to friendship, according to acquaintance, according to association, according to having the same preceptor, or according to having the same teacher— saying, 'Give soup here, give rice there'— this is called 'directing.
By those bhikkhus means by the bhikkhus who are eating."
"That bhikkhunī" refers to whichever bhikkhunī is giving directions.
That bhikkhunī should be dismissed by those bhikkhus with these words: "Withdraw for now, sister, until the bhikkhus have finished eating."
If even a single monk accepts [food] with the thought, "I will eat it, I will consume it," when he has not been invited, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
If one does not stop a person who is fully ordained and who is giving directions, perceiving her to be fully ordained, there is an offense entailing confession.
If she is fully ordained, but he is uncertain of it, and he does not prevent her from instructing [a man], there is an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*).
If she is fully ordained, but he perceives her as not fully ordained, and he does not prevent her from instructing [a man], there is an offense entailing confession.
If she is fully ordained on only one side [of the dual ordination], and he does not prevent her from instructing [a man], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If she is not ordained, but he perceives her as ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she is not ordained, but he is uncertain of it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she is not ordained, and he perceives her as not ordained, there is no offense.
There is no offense if she causes her own meal to be given but does not give it herself,
or if she gives the meal of others but does not cause it to be given.
He causes what has not been given to be given;
he causes it to be given where it has not been given;
he causes it to be given equally to all.
If a trainee nun gives directions,
or a novice nun gives directions—
in all cases, except for the five kinds of food— there is no offense.
"In the case of one who is insane,
or in the case of the first offender.
The second training rule on offenses entailing acknowledgment is concluded.
